newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS -Market crazy for downside dlr/yen strikes.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS -Market crazy for downside dlr/yen strikes.

text.p: Investors piled into dollar/yen options with downside strikes in Europe on Wednesday, sending risk reversals deep into yen call territory, traders said.
The one-month dollar/yen risk reversal -- a gauge of market preference for calls or puts -- shot up to 2.3/2.7 percent in favour of yen calls from 1.9/2.3 in morning Europe.

Dealers reported panic buying of dollar/yen downside strikes amid concerns spot would lurch downhill. Those nerves were especially intense ahead of the G7 summit on June 20-22, where players fear Japan's mushrooming trade surplus will provoke friction with the U.S. and stern exchange rate rhetoric.

This extreme bias in the risk reversal was seen last week when dollar/yen plumbed seven-month lows. Before then, such risk reversal levels had not been seen since August 1995 when central banks intervened to prop the dollar when it was trading just above 85 yen.
Dollar/yen volatility climbed to 13.1/13.4 percent in the one-month by 1400 GMT from 12.7/13.1 in late Europe on Tuesday.

Spot dollar/yen slipped to 112.88/98 from late yesterday's 113.27/37. Recent weeks have seen a sharp decline in the U.S. unit, which has fallen from a 55-month peak of 127.45 yen on May 1 to a low of 110.52 on June 11 -- its weakest level since last September.
"In the last two or three weeks we've seen a big drop...so the market's concerned we could see another move to the downside, maybe even break 110," said an options dealer at a U.S. bank in London.

Traders reported strong interest in one-month dollar/yen options with strikes as low as 109. Further along the vol curve, recent days had seen demand for six-month yen calls with strikes in the 105/106 area, said one dealer at a UK bank.
Dollar/yen vols were likely to remain firm ahead of this weekend's G7 summit in Denver, Colorado, traders said.

"The last couple of times before G7 meetings, dollar/yen volatilities have gone into G7 progressively higher, so the week before they get bought and bought and then on the Monday they're lower again," said a senior options dealer at a U.S. bank here.
